related.name: Audio Dynamic Range & Data Rate Calculator

guidance: A single-boundary acoustic estimate for speaker placement, not a measurement: every nearby surface adds its own comb, and the depth of a notch depends on how strong that reflection is.
method: The reflection is modelled as an image source behind the boundary, so the reflected path is longer than the direct path by twice the perpendicular distance d from the loudspeaker to that surface. Cancellation occurs where that difference is half a wavelength, which puts the first null at f = c / (4d) with c = 343 m/s at 20 degrees Celsius; measured path differences, as GIK Acoustics describes, give the same result from c / (2 x difference). The page reports the first null, the second and third notches at 3f and 5f, the reinforcement peaks at 2f and 4f, the spacing between nulls, the reflected path difference, the wavelength at the first null and the reflection delay in milliseconds. It also inverts the same relation to give the largest distance at which the first null still lands at or above a target frequency, so the page can say whether the speaker is close enough to the boundary for the notch to sit above that frequency. Distances accept centimetres or inches (exactly 2.54 cm per inch) and are converted both ways; the speed of sound is fixed at its 20 degree value, which moves by about 3 percent between 15 and 25 degrees. The model assumes one flat hard boundary and a single specular reflection: rear ports, furniture, an angled wall, an off-axis listener and the other boundaries each add their own comb, and the depth of a notch depends on how strong that reflection is against the direct sound. Because the direct and reflected sounds arrive together, an equaliser boost at the notch lifts the reflection too, so placement and absorption are the only fixes. Inputs allow 1 to 1000 cm or 0.4 to 393.7 in and a target from 20 to 500 Hz; blank, non-numeric and out-of-range values are refused with an actionable message. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Arqen, Speaker Placement 101: How to Fight Boundary Interference — the SBIR notch from quarter-wavelength cancellation, f = c / 4d, and the close-to-wall or far-from-wall placement rules
GIK Acoustics, What is Speaker Boundary Interference Response (SBIR)? — dip frequency from the reflected path difference, c / (2 x difference), and a notch depth of up to about 12 dB
